title: MPs for Sale? Returns to Office in Postwar British Politics
research_question: Do politicians personally benefit financially from holding legislative office, and if so, by how much? Does the magnitude of this financial return vary systematically across political parties with different organizational and financing structures?
data_description: The authors construct an original dataset on parliamentary candidates in the United Kingdom who first stood for the House of Commons in general elections between 1950 and 1970. Biographical information (full name, year/month of birth, gender, secondary schooling, university, occupation, titles of nobility, electoral results) was digitized from The Times Guide to the House of Commons for each election in this period, covering roughly 5,729 candidates. Dates of death were located in UK genealogical death registries (post-1984), and gross estate values at death (probate values, in real 2007 GBP) were retrieved from the probate calendars at First Avenue House in London. The estimation sample comprises 427 relatively competitive Conservative and Labour candidates (165 winners, 262 losers). Supplementary data include directorships from the Directory of Directors (1983) and outside interests reported in the Register of Members' Interests (1975, 1990, 2007). The unit of observation is the individual candidate.
institutional_context: Postwar British MPs received modest official salaries but were permitted to hold outside employment while serving, including corporate directorships, paid parliamentary consultancies, journalism, legal practice, and trade union sponsorships. Disclosure of outside financial interests was not required until 1975, and amounts were not disclosed until the mid-1990s, leaving substantial scope for MPs to monetize their political positions. Conservative and Labour parties were organized very differently: Labour was financed largely by a small number of trade unions that directly sponsored candidates, shaped candidate selection through local constituency councils, and demanded loyalty from sponsored MPs, while the Conservative Party drew funding from diffuse individual and corporate contributors with no dominant constituency. Conservative MPs frequently came from law and business and commonly accepted directorships and consultancies with private firms seeking political access. Public concern about MPs trading political influence for private gain grew throughout this period, culminating in scandals in the 1990s.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The main finding is that serving as an MP does not lead to significant financial gains compared to those who narrowly lost.
